title: Wildlife casualty — adult fox: near-total hair loss and thickened skin
presentation: Adult male red fox caught by a wildlife rescue after being seen in daylight in a garden, emaciated, with almost no coat, thickened crusted skin and constant scratching.

stages.title: Assess the casualty
stages.briefing: Emaciated, BCS 1/5. Alopecia over 80% of the body with thickened, lichenified, crusted skin, worst on the tail base, hocks and ears. Excoriations from self-trauma, secondary pyoderma with a rancid odour. Active in daylight, poor flight response. Temperature 39.4°C. Other foxes in the area reported similarly affected by the rescue.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to sarcoptic mange?

options.label: Crusted, lichenified alopecia worst at tail base, hocks and ears
options.detail: The distribution sarcoptic mange favours in foxes

options.label: Intense self-trauma from pruritus
options.detail: Sarcoptes is severely pruritic

options.label: Other foxes in the same area affected
options.detail: A contagious, population-level parasite

options.label: Daylight activity with a poor flight response
options.detail: Marks debility, not a specific disease

options.label: Temperature 39.4°C
options.detail: Consistent with secondary infection, non-specific

stages.explanation: Distribution is the diagnosis in mange: tail base, hocks and ears, with crusting and lichenification, is sarcoptic mange in a fox, and the pruritus separates it from the demodicosis and dermatophytosis that also cause alopecia. Daylight activity in a fox tells you it is debilitated and unafraid, which matters for handling and for prognosis rather than for diagnosis.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: The fox is sedated for handling and sampling.

options.label: Deep skin scrapes from multiple sites in mineral oil
options.detail: Sarcoptes mites, eggs and faecal pellets

options.label: Skin cytology from crusted and excoriated areas
options.detail: Grades the secondary bacterial and yeast infection

options.label: Fungal culture or dermatophyte PCR
options.detail: Dermatophytosis is the differential and a zoonosis

options.label: Haematology and biochemistry with total protein
options.detail: Anaemia, protein loss and organ function before treatment

options.label: Faecal parasitology
options.detail: Concurrent endoparasites are near-universal in casualties

options.label: Allergen-specific IgE serology
options.detail: No role in a wildlife casualty with this distribution

options.label: Skin biopsy as the first-line test
options.detail: Scrapes are quicker, cheaper and usually diagnostic

stages.explanation: Deep scrapes from several sites are what find Sarcoptes, and taking them from more than one place matters because mite numbers are patchy even in severe disease. Cytology decides whether an antibiotic is needed, and the dermatophyte test is run partly for the people handling the animal. Bloods matter before treating an emaciated casualty.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Deep scrapes: numerous Sarcoptes scabiei mites, eggs and faecal pellets at three of five sites. Cytology: cocci with neutrophils, moderate Malassezia. Dermatophyte PCR negative. Haematology: mild non-regenerative anaemia, neutrophilia. Biochemistry: total protein 44 g/L with albumin 18 g/L, urea and creatinine normal. Faecal: Toxocara and Uncinaria eggs. Body weight 4.1 kg against an expected 6.5–7.5 kg.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Severe sarcoptic mange
options.detail: Mites, eggs and faecal pellets on scrapes

options.label: Secondary bacterial and Malassezia infection
options.detail: Cocci, neutrophils and yeast on cytology

options.label: Protein loss and emaciation are life-limiting
options.detail: Albumin 18 g/L at 4.1 kg

options.label: Concurrent endoparasitism needs treating
options.detail: Toxocara and Uncinaria eggs

options.label: Dermatophytosis is contributing
options.detail: PCR negative

options.label: Renal disease explains the low albumin
options.detail: Urea and creatinine are normal

stages.explanation: The mites confirm the diagnosis, but the albumin of 18 g/L is what determines whether this fox survives treatment: protein has been lost through damaged skin for weeks, and an acaricide alone does not fix that. Ruling out dermatophytosis matters for the volunteers handling him, and the worm eggs are a treatable extra drain on a starving animal.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Numerous Sarcoptes scabiei on deep scrapes, secondary bacterial and Malassezia infection, albumin 18 g/L with total protein 44 g/L, emaciation at 4.1 kg, concurrent Toxocara and Uncinaria, dermatophyte PCR negative.

options.label: Severe sarcoptic mange with secondary infection, protein loss and emaciation
options.detail: The parasite and the systemic state it has produced

options.label: Dermatophytosis
options.detail: PCR negative

options.label: Demodicosis
options.detail: Scrapes identified Sarcoptes, and the distribution and pruritus fit mange

options.label: Nutritional alopecia from starvation
options.detail: Starvation does not produce crusted pruritic lesions full of mites

options.label: Allergic dermatitis
options.detail: Not a meaningful diagnosis in a wild fox with confirmed mites

stages.explanation: The full diagnosis is what makes the rehabilitation plan realistic: acaricidal treatment, antibacterial and antifungal therapy for the skin, anthelmintics, and above all weeks of nutritional support before release is even discussed. It also raises the local picture — mange spreading through an urban fox population is a public and wildlife health observation worth recording.
